test.founder_literal_class_note: the founder literal threshold (city lost >= 1.9M 1990->2024) classifies ZERO cities in this 11-metro cohort (the biggest city-grain loser = Detroit at -383,939); the 1.9M threshold reads on the METRO grain only for the New Orleans MSA (-343k over 2000->2024, still short) — so the literal class is honest-NULL here and the test carried on the percent-decline lens (>= -25% = Detroit/St. Louis/New Orleans) + raw correlation lenses.

verdict.headline: FLIGHT DOES NOT EXPLAIN THE CEILING ORDER. The p90-ceiling rank order tracks NOTHING in the population lanes (best r = 0.53 with raw city-pop DELTA; every percent-change lens r <= 0.30). The two highest ceilings (Boston $168,090, NY $166,080) GAINED city population 1990-2024 (+17.4% each), while the deepest decliners (Detroit -37.4%, St. Louis -29.3%, New Orleans -26.9%) sit mid-table p50-$115k-127k, and Memphis — barely changed (+0.6%) — owns the LOWEST ceiling $100,640.
verdict.founder_literal_class: NULL (no metro in the cohort lost >= 1.9M residents city-grain 1990->2024)

secondary_25pct_class.read: the flight-25 group p90 ceilings sit $12,396 BELOW the rest — direction the hypothesis wanted, but the group is n=3 and the two biggest ceiling outliers (Boston/NY) are non-flight growth cities, so the class explains the MIDDLE of the ladder, NOT its top.

verdict.metro_lens: metro-grain 2000->2024 percent-change correlates even WORSE with the ceiling (r=0.095) — the metro-subset lens REJECTS the flight-shape hypothesis harder than the city lens.
verdict.strongest_signal: raw 1990->2024 city-pop DELTA vs p90 (r=+0.53): BIG metros have higher ceilings — a scale/size effect, not a flight effect.
